title: The Fermi paradox: where is everybody?

figure.alt: A panorama of the Milky Way: a bright band of hundreds of billions of stars, crossed by dark dust lanes.
figure.caption: Our galaxy, the Milky Way, seen from Earth: hundreds of billions of stars.

question: Our galaxy has hundreds of billions of stars, and most of them have planets. It is over 13 billion years old. Even a spacecraft travelling at 1% of the speed of light could cross it in about 10 million years: less than 0.1% of the galaxy's age. So if intelligent life is common, why have we found no sign of anyone else?
thinking:
Nobody knows. The suggested answers fall into three groups.

  • Life, or intelligent life, is rare. Perhaps the conditions for life are unusual, or some step (from simple cells to complex life, or surviving your own technology) almost never happens. This is sometimes called a "Great Filter".
  • They exist, but we can't detect them. Signals spread out and get weaker with the inverse-square law, so a radio transmission from even a nearby star would be extremely faint. And we've only been listening for a few decades: our own radio broadcasts have reached stars within about 100 light-years, a tiny part of a galaxy 100 000 light-years across.
  • They exist, but don't come or don't call. Civilisations might last only a short time, or have no interest in contacting us.

Telescopes now find thousands of planets around other stars, some of them about Earth's size at the right distance for liquid water. That makes the silence more puzzling, not less.
discussion: Our radio signals have travelled about 100 light-years. Treat the galaxy as a disc 100 000 ly across and 1000 ly thick: roughly what fraction of its volume have our signals reached? What does that suggest about the silence?
Which of the suggested explanations could be tested, and how? Is "they exist but hide from us" a scientific hypothesis?
Should we deliberately send messages to other stars? Who should decide?
tok: Is the absence of evidence ever evidence of absence?

title: Olbers' paradox: why is the night sky dark?

figure.alt: The Hubble Ultra Deep Field: a tiny patch of apparently empty sky, crowded with thousands of faint, distant galaxies.
figure.caption: A tiny patch of "empty" sky, photographed for about 11 days by the Hubble Space Telescope. Almost every spot of light is a whole galaxy.
figure.credit: Image: NASA and ESA, Wikimedia Commons, public domain. Resized.

question: Imagine the universe goes on forever, has always existed, and is filled fairly evenly with stars. Then wherever you look, your line of sight must eventually end on the surface of a star. So why isn't the whole night sky as bright as the surface of the Sun?
puzzling: Think of the stars in thin shells around the Earth. A shell twice as far away has an area four times larger, so it contains about four times as many stars. But each of those stars looks four times fainter, by the inverse-square law $b = \dfrac{L}{4\pi d^2}$. So every shell sends us the same amount of light, whatever its distance. With an endless number of shells, the sky should blaze.
thinking:
The paradox is solved, and the dark sky turns out to be evidence about the whole universe.

  • The universe has a finite age (about 13.8 billion years). Light from very distant stars hasn't had time to reach us yet, so we only receive light from a limited region, however large the universe is.
  • Stars don't shine forever. There simply isn't enough starlight in the universe to make every part of the sky as bright as a star's surface.
  • The universe is expanding. Light from distant galaxies is redshifted, so it arrives with less energy.

There's a twist: in one sense the sky is glowing in every direction. The early universe was hot and bright everywhere. That light has been stretched by the expansion into microwaves, the cosmic microwave background, which now matches a black body at about 2.7 K, far too cold for our eyes to see.
discussion: Explain why a finite age solves the paradox even if the universe is infinitely large.
Use Wien's law to find the peak wavelength of the 2.7 K background radiation. Why can't we see it?
The writer Edgar Allan Poe suggested the finite-age answer in 1848, long before there was any evidence for it. What role should imagination play in science?
tok: Can an everyday observation, like a dark night sky, be strong evidence for a theory about the whole universe?

links.title: Why is it dark at night? (minutephysics)

title: The twin paradox: who ends up younger?

figure.alt: A spacetime diagram. The Earth twin's world line goes straight up the time axis for 10 years. The travelling twin's world line goes out to a star 4 light-years away, arriving after 5 years, then turns round and comes back, meeting the Earth twin again at 10 years.
figure.caption: World lines in the Earth's frame: the Earth twin stays put; the travelling twin flies to a star 4 ly away at $0.8c$ and back.

thinkingVideo.title: Twin paradox: the real explanation (no maths)

question: One twin stays on Earth. The other flies to a star 4 light-years away at $0.8c$ and comes straight back. While they move apart, each twin sees the other's clock running slow. So when they meet again, which twin is younger? Surely they can't both be?
thinking:
The travelling twin is younger, and experiments agree.

The situation only looks symmetric. The Earth twin stays in one inertial frame the whole time. The travelling twin doesn't: they turn round and switch from an outward-moving frame to an inward-moving one, and only they feel the acceleration. On a spacetime diagram, the travelling twin's world line is bent, and between the same two events (leaving and returning), a bent world line always has less proper time than a straight one.

In numbers, in the Earth's frame the trip takes 10 years. With $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 0.8^2}} = \dfrac{5}{3}$, the traveller's clock records $\dfrac{10}{5/3} = 6$ years. They come home 4 years younger than their twin.

In 1971, atomic clocks flown around the world on airliners came back differing from identical clocks left on the ground by a few hundred billionths of a second, as relativity predicted.
discussion: Draw the trip on a spacetime diagram. Where is the asymmetry between the twins?
Is the acceleration at the turn-round the cause of the age difference, or just a sign that the two journeys are different?
Is a "paradox" a contradiction in nature, or in our reasoning?
tok: When common sense and a well-tested theory disagree, which should we trust?

title: The arrow of time: why can't you unscramble an egg?

figure.alt: Two boxes of gas particles. In the first, blue particles are on the left and orange on the right, just after a partition is removed. In the second, later, the colours are completely mixed. An arrow forwards in time is solid; an arrow backwards is dashed with a question mark.
figure.caption: Two gases just after the partition is removed, and some time later. Nobody has ever seen the mixed gases separate again.

question: Film two snooker balls colliding and play the film backwards: it still looks perfectly possible. The laws of motion work the same forwards and backwards in time. Yet you never see a smashed egg put itself back together, or milk unmix from tea. If the laws don't care about the direction of time, where does the difference between past and future come from?
thinking:
Part of the answer is well understood. The second law of thermodynamics says the entropy of an isolated system tends to increase, and $S = k_B \ln \Omega$ explains why: a mixed arrangement can happen in vastly more ways (microstates) than a separated one. Nothing forbids the gases from separating again; it's just overwhelmingly unlikely. With the 28 particles in the picture, the chance of finding all the blue ones on the left and all the orange ones on the right at a given moment is about 1 in 300 million. With $10^{23}$ particles, it would never be seen in the lifetime of the universe.

So the arrow of time is statistical. But that raises a deeper question that is still unsolved: for entropy to be increasing everywhere today, the universe must have started in a state of extraordinarily low entropy. Why was the early universe so special? Nobody knows.
discussion: Use the coins idea from B.4: what is the chance that 100 tossed coins all land heads? How does this help explain why gases don't unmix?
If the second law is only true "almost certainly", is it still a law?
We remember the past but not the future. Could that be connected to entropy?
tok: Can a law that is only true with overwhelming probability count as certain knowledge?

links.title: The most misunderstood concept in physics: entropy (Veritasium)

title: Dark matter: what is holding galaxies together?

figure.alt: A graph of the orbital speed of stars against distance from the centre of a spiral galaxy. The expected curve, based on the visible matter, rises and then falls steadily. The measured curve rises and then stays flat out to large distances.
figure.caption: Orbital speeds of stars in a typical spiral galaxy: expected from the matter we can see, and measured.

question: Most of the visible matter in a spiral galaxy is packed near its bright centre, so stars far out should orbit more slowly, just as Neptune orbits the Sun more slowly than the Earth does. But measurements show that the outer stars orbit as fast as the inner ones. Either galaxies contain far more mass than we can see, or our understanding of gravity is wrong on large scales. Which is it?
thinking:
For a circular orbit, $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$, where $M$ is the mass inside the orbit. If the speed stays the same as $r$ increases, $M$ must keep growing in proportion to $r$, even in the dark outer regions where there are few stars. The speeds are measured from the Doppler shift of light and radio waves from the stars and gas.

Most astronomers think galaxies sit inside huge clouds of dark matter: matter that has mass but doesn't emit or absorb light. There is other evidence too, such as the way galaxy clusters bend light from galaxies behind them (gravitational lensing). Altogether there seems to be about five times more dark matter than ordinary matter.

But nobody has ever detected a dark matter particle, despite decades of searching with detectors deep underground. A minority of physicists think gravity itself behaves differently over very large distances. Their ideas explain rotation curves well, but struggle with other evidence. The question is still open.
discussion: Use $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$: if $v$ stays constant as $r$ doubles, what happens to the mass $M$ inside the orbit?
How can scientists be confident something exists when it has never been detected directly?

In the 1800s, odd wobbles in Uranus's orbit led astronomers to predict an unseen planet, and Neptune was found. Odd behaviour in Mercury's orbit led to a predicted planet that was never found; instead, Einstein's new theory of gravity explained it. When should we look for something unseen, and when should we change the theory?
tok: When observations disagree with a theory, how do we decide whether to change the theory or to look for something we have missed?

title: Maxwell's demon: can a tiny gatekeeper beat the second law?

figure.alt: A box of gas divided by a wall with a small trapdoor. A tiny demon sits by the door. Gas molecules move about on both sides, some fast (long orange arrows) and some slow (short blue arrows).
figure.caption: The demon opens the trapdoor only for fast molecules going right and slow molecules going left.

question: A box of gas is divided in two by a wall with a tiny, frictionless trapdoor. Both halves start at the same temperature. A tiny "demon" watches the molecules and opens the door only to let fast ones into the right half and slow ones into the left. Soon the right half is hot and the left half is cold, although the demon has done almost no work. The entropy of the gas has gone down, which the second law says can't happen. So what's wrong?
thinking:
James Clerk Maxwell imagined the demon in 1867, and it took about a century to find the flaw. The answer is that information is physical.

To sort the molecules, the demon has to measure each one's speed and remember it, at least until it decides what to do with the door. Its memory is finite, so sooner or later it must erase old measurements to make room for new ones. In 1961 Rolf Landauer showed that erasing information always transfers energy to the surroundings as thermal energy: at least $k_B T \ln 2$ for every bit, which is about $2.9 \times 10^{-21}$ J at room temperature. That increases the entropy of the surroundings by at least as much as the sorting decreased the entropy of the gas, so the total entropy never falls and the second law survives. In 1982 Charles Bennett used this to show that it is the erasing, not the measuring, that the demon can't avoid.

This is no longer only a thought experiment. In 2012, physicists measured the tiny amount of thermal energy released when a single bit of information was erased, and when the erasing was done slowly enough, it approached Landauer's limit but never went below it.
discussion: Why does the demon need to measure the molecules at all, and why must it eventually forget what it measured?
Calculate $k_B T \ln 2$ at 300 K. Why don't we notice this energy in everyday computers, which erase billions of bits every second?
Can a thought experiment, with no real apparatus, produce new scientific knowledge?
tok: Can a thought experiment that can never be carried out tell us anything about the real world?

links.title: Reversing entropy with Maxwell's demon (PBS Space Time)

title: Why is gravity so weak?

figure.alt: A small horseshoe magnet has lifted a paper clip, which hangs from its poles above the curve of the whole Earth. A long arrow shows the magnet pulling the clip up and a shorter arrow shows the Earth's gravity pulling it down.
figure.caption: A small magnet's pull up on a paper clip beats the gravitational pull down of the entire Earth.

question: A small magnet can lift a paper clip off the table, beating the gravitational pull of the entire Earth. Between two protons, the electric force is about $10^{36}$ times stronger than the gravitational force. Gravity is by far the weakest of the forces. Why is it so weak?
thinking:
Part of the story is well understood: why gravity still rules planets, stars and galaxies. Electric forces can attract or repel, and large objects contain almost equal amounts of positive and negative charge, so their electric forces cancel. Gravity only ever attracts, so every kilogram adds to it. Over large distances it wins simply because nothing cancels it.

But why gravity is so weak in the first place is unsolved. Physicists call it the "hierarchy problem". Some ideas suggest there are extra, very small dimensions of space that gravity spreads into while the other forces can't, which would dilute it. Experiments at the Large Hadron Collider and very precise measurements of gravity over distances below a millimetre have looked for signs of this and so far found none. Others think the strengths of the forces may simply be the way our universe happens to be. Gravity is also the one force that has not yet been combined with quantum physics.

Its weakness makes gravity hard to measure: $G$ is known far less precisely than the other fundamental constants.
discussion: Use $F = \dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r^2}$ and $F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$ to show that the electric force between two protons is about $10^{36}$ times the gravitational force. Why doesn't the distance matter?
If gravity is so weak, why does it control the motion of the planets, rather than electric forces?
Can "that's just how our universe is" ever be a scientific answer?
tok: When is "that's just the way it is" an acceptable answer to a question in science?

links.title: Why is gravity so weak? (Washington University in St. Louis)

title: Where did all the antimatter go?

figure.alt: A gamma-ray photon, drawn as a wavy line, passes close to a nucleus. From that point an electron and a positron spiral away in opposite directions.
figure.caption: A gamma-ray photon turning into an electron and a positron (its antiparticle) close to a nucleus. A magnetic field curves them in opposite directions.

question: Whenever energy turns into matter in an experiment, it makes matter and antimatter in equal amounts: a gamma-ray photon, for example, passing close to a nucleus can become an electron and a positron. If the early universe made matter the same way, there should have been equal amounts of each, and they would have annihilated each other, leaving only radiation. Yet stars, planets and people are made of matter. Where did the antimatter go?
thinking:
Nobody knows. Measurements of the early universe suggest that for roughly every billion particles of antimatter there were a billion and one particles of matter. Almost everything annihilated, and that tiny leftover of matter became everything we see.

For the laws of physics to produce that leftover, matter and antimatter must behave slightly differently. Experiments, for example at CERN, have found small differences in how some particles and their antiparticles decay, but far too small to explain the imbalance. In 2023, the ALPHA experiment at CERN showed that atoms of antihydrogen fall downwards under gravity, with an acceleration consistent with ordinary matter's within the experiment's uncertainty (roughly 30%): no difference there either, so far. The search for a bigger difference continues.

We are also fairly sure there are no galaxies made of antimatter: where antimatter and matter regions met, annihilation would produce gamma rays that we would detect, and we don't see them.
discussion: In β⁺ decay a positron is emitted. Which other particle is emitted with it, and what evidence shows that it must be there? (HL hint: think about the energies of the emitted positrons and conservation of energy.)
Hospitals use positrons every day in PET scans. What happens when a positron meets an electron inside the body, and what is detected?
How can we have evidence about events that happened long before any observer existed?
tok: How can we know about events that happened before there was anyone to observe them?

title: Does hot water freeze faster than cold? The Mpemba effect

figure.alt: An open upright freezer at minus 18 degrees Celsius with two identical beakers of water on a shelf. Steam rises from the left beaker, labelled hot; the right beaker is labelled cold.
figure.caption: Two identical beakers of water go into the same freezer at the same moment: one hot, one cold. Which freezes first?

question: Two identical beakers hold 100 g of water each, one at 80 °C and one at 30 °C, and both go into the same freezer. The hot water has far more thermal energy to lose: cooling it to 0 °C means removing $0.100 \times 4200 \times 80 = 34$ kJ, against 13 kJ for the cooler water, and then each needs another $0.100 \times 3.34 \times 10^5 = 33$ kJ removed to freeze. On the face of it the hot water must take longer, because at some point it has to pass through 30 °C and then do everything the cold water did. Yet in 1963 a Tanzanian school student, Erasto Mpemba, noticed that a hot ice-cream mixture froze before a cold one, and people have been reporting the same thing since Aristotle. Can hot water really freeze faster than cold water, and if so, why?
thinking:
The honest answer in 2026 is: sometimes, under some conditions, and physicists still disagree about why, and even about how to test it.

Mpemba was laughed at by his classmates, but when the physicist Denis Osborne visited his school, he tried the experiment himself, saw the effect, and the two published it together in 1969. Aristotle, Francis Bacon and René Descartes had all written that warmed water freezes more readily, so the claim is old, but so is the difficulty of pinning it down. Many mechanisms have been proposed, and each has been disputed: the hot water evaporates more, so there is less of it left to freeze; it holds less dissolved gas; its stronger convection currents carry warm water to the surface, where it cools faster; its container melts the frost on the freezer shelf and makes better thermal contact; and cold water tends to supercool further below 0 °C before ice forms, which can delay its freezing.

In 2016 Henry Burridge and Paul Linden tested the claim carefully, timing how long water from different starting temperatures took to reach 0 °C. They found no effect at all: the hotter water always took longer, and the apparent effects in earlier reports were small enough to be produced by moving the thermometer by 1 cm. Their conclusion was that "hot water freezes faster" has never been meaningfully demonstrated. Others object that reaching 0 °C is not freezing, and a 2024 study of small drops and a 2025 preprint reported that initially hot water sometimes did solidify first, in one case only when the freezer was barely cold enough for ice to start forming, a process that is itself random. In other words, the dispute is as much about what "frozen" means and how to control the experiment as about the physics.

Meanwhile the idea has taken on a life of its own. In 2017 theorists showed that in some systems a hotter starting state really can reach a cold equilibrium sooner, because it takes a different route through its possible states, and they predicted an inverse effect, where a cold system heats up faster than a warm one. Both have since been seen in experiments on tiny particles in water (2020 and 2022) and in quantum systems (2024–2025). None of that proves the kitchen-freezer version, but it shows that "more energy to lose" is not the whole story of how fast a system cools.

thinkingVideo.title: Hot Water Freezes Either Faster or Slower Than Cold Water

discussion: Design the fairest possible test. What exactly counts as "frozen": the first ice crystal, the surface frozen over, or the whole beaker solid? Where would you put the thermometer, and why did a 1 cm difference matter in the 2016 study? List every variable you would control (volume, container, lid, position in the freezer, dissolved gas, frost on the shelf) and how.

Use $Q = mc\Delta T$ and $Q = mL$ to calculate the total energy that must be removed from each 100 g sample to turn it into ice at 0 °C. If the freezer removes energy at a rate proportional to the temperature difference, sketch temperature–time graphs for both samples. Which assumption would have to fail for the curves to cross?

Burridge and Linden say the effect has never been meaningfully shown; others say they measured the wrong thing. How should science treat a claim that is reported often but can't be reproduced reliably?
tok: If an effect is reported for over two thousand years but can't be reliably reproduced, is it knowledge?

title: Why is the Sun's atmosphere hotter than its surface?

figure.alt: The Sun drawn as an orange disc, surrounded by short streamers and a faint dashed outer boundary representing the corona. Labels give the surface temperature as about 5800 kelvin and the corona as one to three million kelvin.
figure.caption: The visible surface (photosphere) and the corona above it. Not to scale: the real corona is extremely faint and extends many solar radii outwards.

question: The Sun's energy is released by fusion in its core and works its way outwards, so the Sun gets cooler from the centre out: about 15 million K in the core and about 5800 K at the visible surface, the photosphere. Then something odd happens. In the thin outer atmosphere, the corona, the temperature climbs again, to between one and three million kelvin. Thermal energy never flows by itself from a cooler body to a hotter one, so the 5800 K surface cannot simply be heating the corona above it. Where does the corona's energy come from, and why hasn't the question been settled after 80 years?
thinking:
The puzzle was born when the corona's temperature was first measured. During eclipses, astronomers had seen a green spectral line that matched no known element, and for decades it was attributed to a new element, "coronium". In 1939–1941 it was identified as light from iron atoms that had lost 13 of their 26 electrons, which only happens in a gas at around a million kelvin. The corona glows in X-rays for the same reason, and photographs from X-ray telescopes show it shining while the cooler photosphere is dark.

The second law of thermodynamics is not broken, because the energy does not arrive as thermal energy. The Sun's churning surface is threaded by magnetic fields, and the energy is carried upwards by those fields and released in the corona. Two kinds of mechanism are the main candidates. In wave heating, the surface motion shakes the field lines and sends magnetic waves (Alfvén waves) up into the corona, where they dissipate. In nanoflares, proposed by Eugene Parker in 1988, tangled field lines snap and reconnect in countless tiny bursts, each far too small to see individually. The power needed is modest, roughly a kilowatt for each square metre of the Sun's surface, about one part in fifty thousand of what the Sun radiates, which is one reason the answer is hard to pin down: the heating is a small effect hidden in a violent environment.

Two spacecraft are now testing the ideas directly. NASA's Parker Solar Probe, launched in 2018, became the first spacecraft to fly through the corona in 2021 and on 24 December 2024 passed about 6.1 million km above the surface at 192 $\text{km s}^{-1}$, the closest and fastest any spacecraft has been. ESA's Solar Orbiter, launched in 2020, images the corona and its small flares from closer in than Earth. So far the measurements show plenty of waves and plenty of small reconnection events, and most solar physicists now expect that both mechanisms contribute, perhaps in different places. What is still missing is a demonstration that either one delivers enough energy in the right place. The corona is seen as X-rays, not visible light, yet it is so thin, about a hundred million times less dense than the photosphere, that it radiates far less than the surface below it: hotter does not mean brighter.

thinkingVideo.title: Discovering the Sun's Mysteriously Hot Atmosphere

discussion: Use Wien's law, $\lambda_{\text{max}} = \dfrac{2.9 \times 10^{-3}}{T}$, to find the peak wavelength of radiation from the 5800 K photosphere and from a 2 million K corona. Which part of the electromagnetic spectrum is each in? Why does the corona look faint and white in an eclipse photograph but bright in an X-ray image?

Explain why a 5800 K surface could never heat a million-kelvin corona by conduction or radiation alone (thermal energy only ever flows from hotter to cooler by these processes), and why energy carried by magnetic waves or reconnection is different. (Think about how a microwave oven heats food that is hotter than the oven's walls.)
How can you measure the temperature of a gas you can't touch? Suggest at least two methods using spectra (which lines are present, how wide they are) and link each to a part of the course.
tok: A new element was invented to explain the corona's green line. When is it reasonable to explain an observation with something nobody has ever seen?

title: The missing solar neutrinos

figure.alt: The Sun on the left. Dashed lines representing neutrinos stream from it to the right, passing straight through a cross-section of the Earth. On the Earth's far side a mine shaft leads down from the surface to a small tank deep underground.
figure.caption: Neutrinos from the Sun's core pass straight through the Earth. A tank of fluid 1.5 km down a mine, shielded from everything else, catches a few of them. Not to scale.

question: The Sun shines by the proton–proton chain, which fuses four hydrogen nuclei into one helium nucleus and releases two positrons, two neutrinos and about 27 MeV of energy. Light takes tens of thousands of years to struggle out of the Sun's interior, but neutrinos interact so weakly that they leave the core in about two seconds and reach Earth eight minutes later: around $6 \times 10^{14}$ pass through every square metre of you every second. From 1968, Ray Davis counted them with 380 $\text{m}^3$ of dry-cleaning fluid 1.5 km down a gold mine in South Dakota, where a neutrino occasionally turned a chlorine nucleus into radioactive argon. He found about one third of the number John Bahcall's model of the Sun predicted, and kept finding it for 25 years. Was the detector wrong, was the Sun wrong, or were the neutrinos themselves doing something nobody expected?
thinking:
The neutrinos were changing type on the way. It took more than 30 years to be sure.

Davis's tank produced about one argon atom every two days, which he extracted and counted with heroic care; the prediction was roughly three times that. Most physicists assumed that one of the two men had made a mistake. The experiment was checked and rebuilt, and Bahcall's solar model was recalculated as better data arrived on nuclear reaction rates and on the Sun's own vibrations (helioseismology), which probe its interior temperature. Both held firm. From the late 1980s Masatoshi Koshiba's Kamiokande detector in Japan, a tank of water watched by light sensors, saw the same shortfall and, for the first time, showed that the neutrinos really were coming from the direction of the Sun.

The way out had been suggested in the late 1960s by Bruno Pontecorvo: if neutrinos have mass, a neutrino created as an electron neutrino can later be found as a muon or tau neutrino. Davis's chlorine could detect only electron neutrinos, so if two thirds of them had changed type, his count would come out at a third. In 1998 Super-Kamiokande showed that neutrinos made in the atmosphere change type as they cross the Earth. Then, in 2001–2002, the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory in Canada, using 1000 tonnes of heavy water 2 km underground, counted the Sun's electron neutrinos and all three types separately. The electron neutrinos were about a third of the total, and the total matched Bahcall's prediction. Both Davis and Bahcall had been right all along.

The consequence was bigger than the puzzle. The Standard Model of particle physics had assumed neutrinos were massless; changing type requires mass, so this was the first firm evidence of physics beyond the Standard Model. (In the Sun the change is also affected by the dense matter the neutrinos pass through, which goes beyond the course.) Davis and Koshiba shared half of the 2002 Nobel Prize in Physics for detecting cosmic neutrinos; Takaaki Kajita (Super-Kamiokande) and Arthur McDonald (SNO) shared the 2015 prize for showing that neutrinos change type and therefore have mass.

thinkingVideo.title: The solar neutrino problem | Even Bananas 08

discussion: In beta-minus decay an antineutrino is emitted; in beta-plus decay a neutrino is. The first step of the proton–proton chain is $^1\text{H} + {}^1\text{H} \rightarrow {}^2\text{H} + e^+ + \nu_e$. Which conservation laws make the positron and the neutrino necessary, and why can the neutrino escape the Sun while the positron cannot?

Why wasn't Bahcall's prediction simply abandoned when the experiment disagreed with it for 25 years? What other evidence about the Sun's core had to agree with the model, and what would have happened to our understanding of fusion in stars if the Sun really were producing a third of the expected neutrinos?

Explain how a tank deep underground can "see" the Sun's core when it cannot see the Sun itself, and why detectors are built underground rather than on the surface. Why do the properties that make neutrinos hard to detect also make them useful?
tok: For 30 years a careful experiment contradicted a careful theory. How long should scientists keep trusting both before giving one up?

title: What counts as a measurement? Schrödinger's cat and the measurement problem

figure.alt: On the left a single photon, drawn as a blue dot, heads towards a barrier with two slits. On the right a small detector box labelled click. Between them sits a large sealed box with a closed lid and a question mark on its front.
figure.caption: A single photon reaches the two slits; a detector on the far side clicks or doesn't; the sealed box's fate depends on that click. At which step does "both slits" become "one place"? Not to scale.

question: Send photons (or electrons) through a double slit one at a time and the dots on the screen still build up an interference pattern, so each one must in some sense pass through both slits. Quantum theory describes it as a superposition of the two paths. Yet every time it arrives, it is detected in one place. The theory's rules say the superposition "collapses" when a measurement is made, but they do not say what a measurement is, or why the detector, which is also made of atoms, is not itself put into a superposition of "clicked" and "not clicked". In 1935 Erwin Schrödinger made the point with a sealed box: wire a cat's fate to a quantum event with a 50% chance, and the rules seem to describe the cat as both alive and dead until someone opens the lid. Where, and why, does the superposition end?
thinking:
There is no agreed answer, ninety years on. The physics that is agreed is called decoherence, worked out from the 1970s onwards. Anything bigger than a few atoms is constantly bumped by air molecules, photons and thermal vibrations, and every bump records which path the object took. Once that record exists, the two paths can no longer interfere, and this happens in an unimaginably short time for anything the size of a dust grain, let alone a cat. Decoherence explains why we never see large superpositions. What it does not explain is why one particular outcome happens rather than the other: that is the measurement problem proper, and it is still open.

Physicists have offered several interpretations. The Copenhagen view treats collapse as a rule you apply when you measure and declines to say more. Many-worlds says there is no collapse: both outcomes happen and the detector, the cat and you branch along with them. Pilot-wave theory says the particle always has one position, guided by a wave that goes through both slits. Objective-collapse theories add a tiny random collapse to the equations, so that big objects collapse by themselves. These give identical predictions for every experiment done so far (objective-collapse theories differ only for objects far larger than any yet tested), which is why the argument has not been settled by data.

Experiment is slowly closing in from the other side, by making superpositions bigger. In 2019 a Vienna group showed interference with molecules of about 2000 atoms (mass about $2.5 \times 10^4$ u), and in 2025 the same group reported interference with sodium clusters of several thousand atoms, over $1.7 \times 10^5$ u, published in Nature in 2026. Tiny mechanical oscillators have been put into quantum states too. Objective-collapse theories predict that interference must fail at some size; so far it hasn't, and the limits on those theories tighten each year. A cat is still about $10^{22}$ times heavier than the record.
discussion: In a double-slit experiment with one electron at a time, what is actually seen on the screen after one electron, after a hundred, and after a million? What does the pattern tell you about each single electron, and what does the single dot tell you?

The 2019 molecules had a mass of about $2.5 \times 10^4$ u and moved at roughly $250\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Estimate their de Broglie wavelength, and explain why interference with such objects is so hard to show.
If several interpretations predict the same results in every experiment, is choosing between them a job for physics at all? What kind of evidence could decide it?
tok: If two theories make identical predictions, can one of them still be more true than the other?

title: Ball lightning: real, rare and unexplained

figure.alt: A storm cloud with rain and an orange lightning bolt on the left. On the right a house with an open window, and a glowing yellow ball drifting in through the window.
figure.caption: A typical report: just after a lightning strike, a glowing ball the size of a football drifts about for a few seconds, sometimes through an open window, then vanishes. Not to scale; the glow colour is as witnesses describe it.

question: For centuries people have described the same thing: during a thunderstorm, a glowing ball, usually 10 to 30 cm across, appears near the ground, drifts about slowly for a few seconds, sometimes passes through a window or along a wire, and then fades or pops. There are thousands of such accounts, including from scientists and pilots. Ordinary lightning lasts less than a millisecond and we understand it well; a glowing ball that hangs in the air for seconds should cool and disperse almost instantly. What is ball lightning, and why can't we make it?
thinking:
Honestly, we don't know, and until recently we weren't even sure it existed. Almost all the evidence is eyewitness testimony, which is hard to use: people are startled, estimates of size and distance are unreliable, and some reports are probably afterimages, St Elmo's fire or ordinary lightning seen oddly. Physicists want measurements they can repeat, and ball lightning refuses to appear on demand.

The best data so far came by luck. In July 2012 a team from Northwest Normal University was recording ordinary lightning on the Qinghai plateau in China with a spectrometer and a high-speed camera when a strike about 900 m away produced a glowing ball that lasted about 1.5 s and drifted about 10 to 15 metres. Their spectrum, published in 2014 by Cen, Yuan and Xue, showed emission lines of silicon, iron and calcium: the main elements of soil, not of air. That supports a hypothesis proposed by John Abrahamson and James Dinniss in 2000: a strike vaporises silicon compounds in the soil, the vapour condenses into a cloud of nanoparticles, and the slow oxidation of those particles, burning, keeps the ball glowing for seconds. Other hypotheses include a plasma held together by its own currents, and microwaves trapped inside a plasma shell.

None has been confirmed. Laboratory discharges usually make glowing plasmoids that last a fraction of a second. Arcs struck on silicon have produced small glowing balls that lasted several seconds (2007), the best support so far for the burning-soil idea, but they were only a few centimetres across, and nobody has produced one that drifts through a window. Even the one spectrum is a single event; it could be one kind of ball lightning, or something else that happened to look like it. The puzzle stays open because the evidence is still mostly anecdotal.
discussion: Thousands of people say they have seen ball lightning. Why is that not enough to count as scientific evidence, and what would the Qinghai recording need (more of what?) before physicists accept the burning-soil explanation?

A lightning strike carries a current of tens of kiloamperes for less than a millisecond. Estimate the charge transferred, then the energy if the potential difference is about $10^8$ V. How much of it would have to end up in a 20 cm ball to keep it glowing for 5 s at, say, 100 W?

Any successful model must respect physics you know: a hot gas expands and cools, a plasma conducts and is pulled by magnetic fields, and energy must come from somewhere. Which of these makes a ball lasting several seconds hardest to explain?
tok: When does a large number of eyewitness reports become knowledge, and when does it stay a story?

title: The black hole information paradox

figure.alt: A black disc with a dashed ring around it, labelled event horizon, sits in the middle of a tilted orange ring that represents the accretion disc. A blue book falls in from the top left. Faint dashed wavy lines leave the hole, labelled radiation out, very faint.
figure.caption: A book falls past the event horizon. Hawking radiation leaks out over an enormous time, but it seems to carry none of the book's words. The accretion disc is glowing gas on its way in. Not to scale.

question: Nothing that crosses a black hole's event horizon can come back out: the escape speed there is the speed of light. In 1974 Stephen Hawking showed that, because of quantum effects near the horizon, a black hole nevertheless glows very faintly, loses mass and eventually evaporates completely. But his calculation said the radiation is purely thermal, the same whatever fell in: a star, a book, or a bag of sand of the same mass. So when the hole has gone, every detail of what fell in has gone with it. Quantum mechanics insists that information is never destroyed: from the complete present state you can always, in principle, work out the past. Does a black hole destroy information, and if not, how does it get out?
thinking:
Two things are not in doubt. Classically, anything inside the Schwarzschild radius $R = \dfrac{2GM}{c^2}$ cannot escape: putting $v_{esc} = c$ into the escape-speed formula gives $R \approx 3$ km for the mass of the Sun (beyond the course, the exact answer needs general relativity, but it gives the same number). And Hawking's radiation is accepted by almost everyone, although it has never been detected: a solar-mass black hole would have a temperature of about $6 \times 10^{-8}$ K, far colder than the $2.7$ K of the cosmic microwave background, so for now it absorbs more than it emits. Its evaporation time would be around $10^{67}$ years, when the universe is $1.4 \times 10^{10}$ years old.

Hawking himself first argued that information really is lost. Most physicists came to disagree, and he changed his mind in 2004, but nobody could show how the information escapes. A big step came in 2019: Geoffrey Penington, and separately Ahmed Almheiri, Netta Engelhardt, Donald Marolf and Henry Maxfield, used new methods to calculate how the "amount of information" in the radiation changes as the hole evaporates. They found the curve Don Page had predicted in 1993 for a hole that does not destroy information: the radiation starts out looking random, but after about half the hole's lifetime it begins to carry the details of what fell in, in a form so scrambled that only an impossibly complete measurement could read them.

That convinced many people that information survives. But the calculations work in simplified models, they say little about what the mechanism is physically, and some physicists still question what they really show. There is no experiment, and none in sight, so this is a puzzle argued out entirely with theory, in a region, the horizon, where our two best theories, quantum mechanics and general relativity, have not yet been made to agree.

thinkingVideo.title: Why Black Holes Could Delete The Universe – The Information Paradox

discussion: Use $v_{esc} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{r}}$ to find the radius at which the escape speed from a body of the Sun's mass ($2.0 \times 10^{30}$ kg) would equal $c$. Compare it with the Sun's actual radius. Why does "escape speed equals $c$" make a black hole black?
Burn a book, and physicists say its information still exists in principle, in the smoke, ash and light. What does "information" mean here, and why is a black hole different from a fire?

Hawking radiation from any real black hole is far too faint to measure, and the evaporation would take $10^{67}$ years. Is a prediction that can't be tested within the lifetime of the universe still science? What would a Popperian say?
tok: Can a claim be scientific knowledge if no possible experiment could show it to be wrong?

title: Can a black hole be less dense than water?

figure.alt: The inner Solar System seen from above: the Sun at the centre with the orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars drawn to scale. A dashed orange circle just outside Mars's orbit marks the event horizon of a black hole of 100 million solar masses.
figure.caption: The event horizon of a black hole of 100 million solar masses, drawn to the same scale as the planets' orbits (Earth's is blue). It reaches about 2 au from the centre, just beyond Mars. The Sun and planets are not to scale.

question: A black hole is usually pictured as matter crushed to an unimaginable density. Yet the biggest black holes at the centres of galaxies, hundreds of millions or billions of times the Sun's mass, have an average density lower than water, and the very largest are less dense than the air you are breathing. How can something that not even light can escape from be less dense than a swimming pool?
thinking:
The puzzle dissolves once you see how the size of a black hole depends on its mass. In D.1 the escape speed from a sphere of mass $M$ and radius $r$ is $v_{esc} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{r}}$. Set this equal to the speed of light and solve for the radius: $r = \dfrac{2GM}{c^2}$. This is the Schwarzschild radius, the radius of the event horizon. (Strictly, a black hole is a prediction of general relativity, not of Newton's gravity, and the proper calculation was made by Karl Schwarzschild in 1916, but the simple argument happens to give exactly the right answer. John Michell had reached a similar conclusion about "dark stars" as early as 1783.)

The key is that the radius grows in proportion to the mass: double the mass and the horizon doubles in radius. The volume inside the horizon grows as $r^3$, so as $M^3$, and the average density $\dfrac{M}{\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3}$ falls as $\dfrac{1}{M^2}$. For one solar mass ($1.99 \times 10^{30}$ kg): $r = \dfrac{2 \times 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 1.99 \times 10^{30}}{(3.00 \times 10^{8})^2} = 2.95$ km, and the average density is $\dfrac{1.99 \times 10^{30}}{\frac{4}{3}\pi (2950)^3} = 1.9 \times 10^{19}$ $\text{kg m}^{-3}$, about $10^{16}$ times denser than water. Now scale up. A hole of $10^{8}$ solar masses has a horizon $10^{8}$ times bigger, $2.95 \times 10^{8}$ km or 1.97 au (just beyond Mars's orbit), and an average density $10^{16}$ times smaller: about $1.9 \times 10^{3}$ $\text{kg m}^{-3}$, roughly twice that of water. The black hole at the centre of the galaxy M87, photographed by the Event Horizon Telescope in April 2019, has a mass of about $6.5 \times 10^{9}$ solar masses. Its horizon has a radius of $1.9 \times 10^{10}$ km, about 128 au, four times the radius of Neptune's orbit, and its average density is $\dfrac{1.9 \times 10^{19}}{(6.5 \times 10^{9})^2} \approx 0.4$ $\text{kg m}^{-3}$: about a third of the density of air at sea level.

So what does "density" mean here? It is the mass divided by the volume enclosed by the horizon, and that is a slightly sneaky quantity. As far as our theories can say, the mass is not spread evenly through that volume; it has collapsed towards the centre, where general relativity breaks down and nobody knows what happens. The horizon is not a surface made of anything: it is simply the boundary beyond which no path leads back out. The low average density does tell you something real, though. The pull of gravity at the horizon, and in particular the difference in pull between your head and your feet (the tidal effect), gets weaker the bigger the hole. At the horizon of a one-solar-mass hole that difference would be around $10^{10}$ $\text{m s}^{-2}$, enough to stretch an astronaut into a thread long before they arrived. At the horizon of M87's hole it is about $5 \times 10^{-10}$ $\text{m s}^{-2}$, far too small to feel. You could cross the horizon of a supermassive black hole without noticing anything special at that moment, and only the fact that you could never get out again would tell you where you were.

The 2019 image fits this picture well. The dark shadow at its centre is about two and a half times the diameter of the horizon (light that passes close to the hole is bent into it), and its size matched what general relativity predicted for a hole of M87's measured mass. A second image, of the much smaller black hole at the centre of our own galaxy ($4 \times 10^{6}$ solar masses), followed in 2022.

thinkingVideo.title: First Image of a Black Hole!

discussion: The escape-speed argument from D.1 treats light as a projectile slowed by gravity, which is not how light behaves, yet it gives the correct Schwarzschild radius. Does a model that gives the right answer for the wrong reason count as a good model? What would make you trust or distrust it?

A sphere's volume grows as $r^3$ but a black hole's mass only as $r$. Use this to explain, without a calculator, why a black hole of a billion solar masses is less dense than one of a million solar masses, and by what factor.

A stellar remnant heavier than about 1.4 solar masses cannot be a white dwarf (the Chandrasekhar limit), and a neutron star above roughly 2 to 3 solar masses must collapse further (the Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit). Stellar black holes therefore form at enormous densities. How, then, can the universe contain black holes of billions of solar masses with the density of air? What do you think they must have done since they formed?
tok: We can never observe the inside of a black hole, even in principle. In what sense can a scientific claim about its interior be knowledge?

title: The hiss that arrived four minutes early

figure.alt: A long rectangular aerial, a frame of upright poles strung with wires, standing on a wooden chassis with four wheels on a circular track, under a night sky with stars and the faint band of the Milky Way. An orange arrow shows the frame turning.
figure.caption: Jansky's aerial, about 30 m long, turned once every 20 minutes on a circular track so that it could tell which direction a radio signal came from. Its wires picked up radio waves of wavelength about 15 m. Not to scale.

question: In 1932 Karl Jansky, a young engineer at Bell Telephone Laboratories in New Jersey, was hunting down the sources of static that spoilt transatlantic radio-telephone calls. He built a 30 m aerial on wheels that turned slowly on a circular track, so that he could tell where each kind of noise came from. Thunderstorms were easy to identify. But one faint, steady hiss was odd: it rose and fell once a day, so he first assumed it came from the Sun. Then he noticed that its peak arrived about four minutes earlier each day, by the clock. Why did those four minutes prove that the hiss came from far beyond the Solar System, and why did they start a whole new kind of astronomy?
thinking:
The clue is in two different lengths of day. The ordinary day, 24 hours from noon to noon, is the time the Earth takes to turn until the Sun is back overhead. But while the Earth spins once, it also moves about a degree along its orbit, so it has to turn a little more than one full rotation before the Sun is overhead again. Measured against the distant stars, one full rotation takes only 23 h 56 min 4 s: the sidereal day. It is shorter than the solar day by 3 min 56 s, which is simply 24 hours divided by the 366.24 rotations the Earth makes in a year. (A year of 365.24 solar days contains one extra rotation, because the Earth's orbit itself adds one turn.) So anything fixed among the stars returns to the same place in the sky about four minutes earlier each day by the clock, and any source that keeps to sidereal time cannot be the Sun or anything else in the Solar System.

Jansky's hiss kept sidereal time. A colleague, the astronomer Albert Skellett, pointed out what that meant, and by the end of 1932 Jansky had traced the direction of the peak to the constellation Sagittarius, which lies towards the centre of the Milky Way. He announced the result in April 1933 and published it that October. It was the first detection of radio waves from beyond the Earth, and the source was about 26 000 light years away. Jansky did not know what produced the emission: the main mechanism, synchrotron radiation from fast electrons spiralling in the galaxy's magnetic field, was not worked out until the 1950s. He asked Bell Labs for a larger dish to follow up, but the static did not threaten the telephone service, the Depression was on, and he was moved on to other work. He never returned to astronomy, and died in 1950 aged 44.

The professional astronomers of the day, who worked only with light, largely ignored the discovery. The person who took it up was Grote Reber, a radio amateur who built a 9 m parabolic dish in his back garden in Wheaton, Illinois, in 1937 and made the first maps of the radio sky, confirming that the whole Milky Way glows at radio wavelengths. After the Second World War, radar engineers turned their equipment on the sky and radio astronomy grew fast: the 21 cm line of hydrogen (1951), which maps the gas in galaxies that light cannot see through the dust; quasars; pulsars (1967); the cosmic microwave background (1965, also at Bell Labs, a few kilometres from Jansky's aerial); and in 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope's image of a black hole, made by radio dishes across the Earth working together. Since 1973 the unit of radio flux density has been the jansky, $1 \text{ Jy} = 10^{-26}$ $\text{W m}^{-2}\,\text{Hz}^{-1}$, a reminder of how faint his hiss was.
discussion: Explain why the sidereal day is about four minutes shorter than the solar day, and why that difference adds up to exactly one extra rotation over a year. How could you use a fixed star and a stopwatch to measure the sidereal day yourself?

Jansky found the hiss with an instrument built to solve a telephone problem. How did a pattern in the timing of a signal tell him about its location, before anyone knew what was producing it? Which of the guide's Nature of Science ideas (observations, patterns and trends, evidence) does each step of his reasoning illustrate?

Radio waves of wavelength 15 m have far lower frequency, and far lower photon energy, than visible light. Using what you know about the electromagnetic spectrum and about dust and gas in space (E.5), suggest what radio telescopes can see that optical telescopes cannot, and vice versa.
tok: Jansky was looking for the source of telephone static and found the centre of the galaxy. How much of scientific knowledge comes from noticing what you were not looking for, and can that kind of discovery be planned?
